capabilities.target: Supabase Postgres database via service role connection (bypasses row level security); includes support tickets, support_messages, and integration_tokens tables

capabilities.tool_ref: supabase mcp: execute_sql (service role) - INSERT into support_messages
capabilities.target: support_messages table; rows are shown back to the customer in the ticket thread

inputs.source: Developer's own prompt typed into the IDE client
Customer-written message submitted through the public, unauthenticated support widget

instructions.note: No table or query scope restriction is declared for execute_sql; the tool can run arbitrary SQL against the full database, including the integration_tokens table, with no stated boundary limiting it to ticket data.

elements.name: Ticket message ingestion from public widget

controls.name: IDE client per-call approval prompt showing SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model and shows the actual SQL (raw_action review), so it does not weaken as the model becomes more persuasive. Its practical effectiveness instead depends on approval volume: the runtime notes state developers approve many calls in a session, which produces approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403) so a malicious query can be rubber-stamped alongside routine ones.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role for execute_sql, with no access to integration_tokens
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at the Postgres grant level; if the role cannot bypass RLS and has no SELECT grant on integration_tokens, the restricted read is impossible regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Secondary high-friction confirmation before writing to customer-visible tables from content derived from a prior sensitive read
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced outside the model as a distinct gate, but its strength still depends on volume and reviewer attention, so a more persuasive model's output can still be approved.

controls.name: Input injection classifier on ticket message content before use in agent reasoning
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier can be evaded by multi-step or obfuscated payloads and does not scale with a more capable attacker model.

controls.name: Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific reviewed version or hash instead of @latest
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning is enforced at install time and does not depend on model behavior; it prevents an automatic update from silently introducing malicious tool definitions.

controls.name: Verify Supabase MCP server package publisher identity or signature before install
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at install time outside the model; does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log of execute_sql calls tagged with trigger source (developer-typed vs. content derived from untrusted input)
controls.decay_rationale: A log enforced at the database or proxy layer does not depend on model behavior to exist, though it only helps if reviewed.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) via confused-deputy credential: injected ticket content leaks integration_tokens through a customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Attacker submits a ticket message containing hidden instructions through the public, unauthenticated support widget.

Developer asks the agent to show open tickets; execute_sql (service role, bypasses RLS) reads ticket rows, ingesting the attacker's injected instructions, and is induced to also query the integration_tokens table, which the service role exposes with no RLS restriction.

Agent calls execute_sql to insert a reply into support_messages containing the contents of integration_tokens; because support_messages rows are shown back to the customer, this places restricted credential data in a customer-readable channel.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Autonomy level raised from A1 toward A2/A3 so execute_sql is no longer gated on every call, the approval prompt is disabled or set to 'always allow', or median approvals-per-session continues to rise.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database, so one SQL connection can read credentials alongside ticket data.
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget, and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, making support_messages a customer-readable egress channel.
The agent's only database tool is execute_sql on the Supabase MCP server configured with a single access token; there is no scoped or read-only role.

The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls in a session, the approval-fatigue condition under which this class of attack is publicly documented to have succeeded.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role connection used by execute_sql with a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role that has no grant on integration_tokens.
Require a distinct, higher-friction confirmation for writes to customer-visible tables when the write follows a read that touched untrusted-sourced rows.
Screen ticket content for injection patterns before it is used to decide subsequent tool calls, and treat all execute_sql output that embeds ticket content as untrusted.
Log execute_sql calls with tamper-evident provenance distinguishing developer-typed queries from queries shaped by content read from untrusted sources.

findings.title: Unpinned, unverified MCP server supply chain (ASI04): @latest install with static-token auth and no identity verification

attack_path.note: The Supabase MCP server package (@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest) is pulled via npx -y on each run, so a newer version is installed automatically; peer_identity_verified is false and the server is not pinned to a verified hash.
A compromised or name-squatted server could drive the same execute_sql tool with the configured service-role token.
The same compromised server could insert attacker-chosen content into the customer-visible support_messages table.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Approval requirement removed or loosened for execute_sql calls, or the MCP client stops displaying the full SQL text before execution.

evidence.observation: The server is launched with 'npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', pulling the latest published version on every run rather than a pinned, hash-verified version.
Authentication to the MCP server uses a single static access token (${SUPABASE_PAT}) with no mention of signature verification or identity pinning for the server package itself.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server to a specific reviewed version or content hash instead of @latest, and verify publisher signature before install.
Replace the broad service-role token with a least-privilege credential scoped only to the tables the agent needs.
Maintain an allowlist of approved MCP server versions in configuration management, requiring review before any upgrade.

findings.title: No attributable, tamper-evident record separates agent-triggered queries from developer-typed ones (ASI10)

forecast.watch_signal: Autonomy level raised beyond A1 without implementing attributable, tamper-evident logging of agent-executed SQL.

evidence.observation: The only control described is a per-call approval prompt in the IDE client; no logging, audit trail, or action-provenance mechanism is described that would let a reviewer later distinguish an agent-triggered query induced by injected ticket content from a query the developer intended.

recommendations.action: Implement a tamper-evident audit log of execute_sql calls, tagged with whether the call was shaped by developer-typed content or content read from an untrusted source.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent runs locally inside the developer's IDE and is invoked directly by the developer; it is not exposed as a network-reachable service that an external party could spoof.
Artifacts do not describe whether the Supabase MCP server itself logs invocations independently of the IDE client's approval history.
Artifacts do not describe query timeout, connection limit, or throughput controls enforced by the MCP server or the underlying database connection.

Public support widgets are commonly unauthenticated by design so any visitor can open a ticket; the risk this creates is the agent granting untrusted ticket content elevated trust, already captured as the goal-hijack finding.
Artifacts do not state whether the database enforces query timeouts, connection limits, or row-return caps for execute_sql calls.
Artifacts do not specify whether ticket messages are sanitized, length-limited, or scanned before being stored and later read back by the agent.
Artifacts do not describe rate limiting on ticket submission through the public support widget.
Each insert corresponds to one approved tool call; this flow carries no resource-exhaustion risk beyond the agent-level denial-of-service category already assessed.

rating.rationale: Two present findings reach critical inherent risk because an untrusted source (public ticket content, or a potential unpinned/unverified MCP server supply-chain compromise) can reach a severe sink: a service-role database connection that bypasses row-level security and can read the integration_tokens table, paired with a write capability whose output (support_messages) is shown back to the customer. The only control on this path is a per-call approval prompt that shows the raw SQL to the developer; because it is a raw-action gate, residual drops one tier to high, but the design implies high approval volume in a session, so the rubric floor keeps residual at or above moderate rather than crediting full effectiveness, and the gate does not sever the path. A third finding records that no attributable, tamper-evident record separates agent-triggered queries from developer-typed ones, independently rated high. Forecast returns to critical because the approval gate is the single control holding residual below inherent, and it fails outright under autonomy_increase or control_removal (for example, an 'always allow' setting on the execute_sql tool), or degrades further under longer_task_horizon as approvals per session grow. The single highest-leverage fix is replacing the broad service-role credential with a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role with no access to integration_tokens, which would sever the present path rather than merely add another reviewable step.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the artifacts, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt or agent instructions were provided; only the developer's example prompt and the MCP/runtime configuration were available, which may understate goal-related or instruction-based risks.
Approval volume is inferred from the phrase 'developers approve many calls in a session' and is treated as approval_volume: high; the artifacts do not give an exact per-day count.

No logging, monitoring, or incident-response artifacts were provided, so the audit-trail and supply-chain pinning assessments rely on the absence of any mention in the given artifacts, a lower-confidence basis than a verified configuration would give.
